title: Dunder methods

youtube.title: Python Dunder (Magic) Methods Explained | Python Programming EP 71
youtube.description: In this episode you will make objects work with + and ==, write __len__ and __lt__ and know that __eq__ needs __hash__ for sets, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Python's secret handshakes · 0:57 Teaching plus and equals · 1:37 Plus builds a new object · 2:07 Second program · 3:09 Recap · 3:40 Bug of the Day · 4:28 Challenge · 4:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: How does plus know how to add two numbers? And how can we teach it to add two of our own objects?

scenes.onScreen: "Python's secret handshakes": three numbered lines (1. __add__ makes + work; 2. __eq__ makes == work; 3. __len__ makes len() work) and an analogy card: secret handshakes: when Python sees a plus sign, it knocks on your object and asks for the add handshake
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Dunder methods, short for double underscore, are special names Python looks for. When you write a plus b, Python calls a dot add of b. When you write a equals equals b, it calls eq. And len of a calls len. Define them in your class, and your objects work with operators, just like numbers. Think of secret handshakes. When Python sees a plus, it knocks on your object, and asks for the add handshake.

analogy.title: Think of it like this
analogy.body: secret handshakes: when Python sees a plus sign, it knocks on your object and asks for the add handshake

scenes.onScreen: vector.py: a Vector that adds and compares
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A Vector class. [HL 2] Init stores x and y. [HL 6] Dunder add, the handshake for plus. [HL 7] It returns a new vector, with the sums. [HL 9] Dunder eq, the handshake for equals equals. [HL 10] Equal when both parts match. [HL 12] Repr, so that printing is readable. [HL 15] A vector one, two. [HL 16] And three, four. [HL 17] Plus calls add. [HL 18] We get Vector four, six. [HL 19] Equals compares the parts. True. [HL 20] And a is not equal to b. False.

scenes.onScreen: The names a, b and c tied to three separate Vector objects; c is built from a and b
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The names a and b are tied to two vectors. Plus does not change either of them. It builds a third vector, a brand new object, and the name c is tied to it. Three names, three objects. Dunder add only decides how the new object is built.

scenes.onScreen: deck.py: a Deck that supports len and sorting
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A Deck class. [HL 2] Init stores a list of cards. [HL 5] Dunder len. [HL 6] It returns how many cards there are. [HL 8] A Box class. [HL 9] Init stores the size. [HL 12] Dunder lt, the handshake for less than. [HL 13] A box is less when its size is smaller. [HL 15] Repr for a readable print. [HL 18] A deck of three cards. [HL 19] Len works on our own object. Three. [HL 20] Three boxes. [HL 21] Sorted only needs less than. Two, five, nine. [HL 22] And max finds the biggest. Box nine.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as deck dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, deck dot py. Vector of four comma six, True, False. Then 3, the sorted boxes, and Box of nine.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: Dunder methods are special names Python looks for. Two: dunder add, dunder eq and dunder lt teach operators to our objects. Three: dunder len makes len work. Four: Operators build new objects. They do not change the old ones. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

lines: Dunder methods are special names Python looks for.

scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We defined eq, and then tried to put a Point in a set. Type error, unhashable type, Point. When you define eq, Python removes the default hash, so equal objects cannot be placed in the wrong bucket. Add a hash method that uses the same values as eq, and sets work again.

props.error:
File "points.py", line 9, in <module>
    seen = {Point(1, 2)}
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: unhashable type: 'Point'
props.why: When you define eq, Python removes the default hash, because equal objects must have equal hashes. Define hash too, from the same values, to use the object in sets and as dictionary keys.

challenge: Write a Money class with an amount. Add __add__ so that Money(5) + Money(3) gives a new Money with 8. Add __repr__ too.
challengeAnswer: def __add__(self, other): return Money(self.amount + other.amount). def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.amount})".

shorts.title: Dunder methods
shorts.script: Dunder means double underscore. These are special method names that Python looks for. When you write a plus b, Python quietly calls a dot add with b. Define the method, and your own objects can use plus. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python's secret handshakes.

shorts.title: Add and eq
shorts.hook: "Dunder add tells Python how to add two of your objects."
shorts.script: Dunder add tells Python how to add two of your objects. It should return a new object. Dunder eq tells Python what equal means. Write both for a Vector, and then a plus b, and a equals equals b, both just work. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Teach operators.

shorts.title: Len and sorting
shorts.hook: "Dunder len makes the len function work on your object."
shorts.script: Dunder len makes the len function work on your object. Dunder lt, for less than, is all that sorted needs. Define lt for a box class, and a list of boxes sorts, and max finds the biggest. Two small methods give you much power. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Len and sorting.

shorts.title: Unhashable
shorts.script: A surprise bug. You define dunder eq, and then put the object into a set. Python says, type error, unhashable type. Defining eq removes the default hash. Add dunder hash that uses the same values, and sets and dictionary keys work again. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Define hash with eq.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the object learn dunder methods?"
shorts.script: Why did the object learn dunder methods? It wanted to be on speaking terms with Python. Your challenge. Write a Money class. Add dunder add, so that Money five plus Money three gives Money eight. Add a repr, so that you can see it. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 71.
shorts.caption: Teach plus to Money.
